It has been revealed that arXiv:2608.27754v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) could turn AI models in Biology and other fields into engines of scientific discovery by explaining the superhuman capabilities of those models. We postulate that a latent is useful if we know three things: whether it is coherent, whether it can be described, and whether that description has predictive power. These questions are routinely conflated. We assemble them into a single pipeline and report some practical innovations. First, cross-seed dictionary stability prioritises which latents are worth spending resources to investigate. Second, an intruder-detection task asks whether a latent's activating examples share a recognizable pattern. Third, a separate pass proposes a candidate biological description which we convert into falsifiable predictions which can be tested in silico. Deployed on the Boltz-1 Pairformer trunk, stability prioritisation finds interpretable latents using about 4.4 times fewer latent evaluations each, and at 5.2 times lower measured LLM cost, while recovering over half of them. However, we notice that in our setup the LLM judge is heavily biased towards consistent residue identity and a simple filter that selects for features with high amino-acid identity precision outperforms the stability thresholding. This simpler method has the added benefit of requiring no extra SAE seeds but it remains uncertain if it reflects a genuinely useful heuristic or an limitation of the LLM judge.

Several routes may share an access lane, yet each can offer a view of row segments that the others miss. We introduce CoverShare to learn complementary routes under a fixed action budget. Within Policy Gradient for Parallel State Entropy maximization (PGPSE), CoverShare redistributes auxiliary rewards according to the state coverage lost when each policy is omitted and the number of policies visiting each state. It preserves the pooled entropy objective and total auxiliary reward. We simulated the annotated road network of a 6.7-ha site with 107 observable persimmon scouting units across five zones. At 40 actions per route, six distinct policies covered an expected 17.84 units perinspection, compared with 8.28 for six independent runs of one policy, averaged across eight training seeds. With the same policies trained on 40-action routes, extending each inspection route to 80 and 120 actions raised coverage to 22.52 and 28.38 units. Across seven public discrete-state tasks, CoverShare increased state support by a mean of 16.29% over the team-entropy baseline. Controlled ablations identified leave-one-policy-out coverage as the main contributor to these gains.

In a recent development, arXiv:2608.25846v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Cough acoustics are promising for non-invasive tuberculosis (TB) screening, yet whether machine learning (ML) models capture disease-related acoustics or artifacts of data collection remains unresolved. We evaluated the cross-dataset generalizability of classical ML and deep learning (DL) cough-based TB classifiers across three independent datasets. Despite moderate within-dataset performance (ROC-AUC up to $0.76 \pm 0.06$), both pipelines fail to generalize, with external performance frequently below 0.6, indicating a possible limitation of the data. We further observed that audio representations are organized by recording device and dataset rather than TB status, predicted TB probability tracks country-level prevalence in CODA, and device mismatch degrades transfer while device-diverse training improves it. Additionally, a clinical-variable baseline generalizes more consistently (ROC-AUC $0.65-0.71$), indicating acquisition-specific variability in acoustics is a stronger driver of poor generalizability. High within-dataset performance is not enough. External validation is essential before cough-based TB models are clinically ready.

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (292 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

According to recent reports, arXiv:2608.13087v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Neural combinatorial optimization (NCO) solvers report the best of many sampled solutions per instance, and the sample count is, by convention, identical for every instance. Whether a non-uniform allocation of a fixed total budget would buy anything has not been measured. We measure it, and we audit the measurement itself. First, on in-distribution workloads the allocation headroom is not detectable. Across three pretrained solvers (POMO, AM, SymNCO) on uniform TSP-100, an oracle allocation computed and evaluated on the same stored samples reports a 2.2-2.6% gain with intervals excluding zero; measured out of sample the same gain is indistinguishable from zero (0.457, 0.015, -0.512 percent). Following the customary in-sample procedure, all three solvers would have supported a published 2%-level gain that does not exist. We calibrate this bias against an instance-wise null in which the true gain is zero by construction; over the ranges we test it does not shrink with more samples or more instances. Second, the same correction that removes the phantom gains preserves a real one. Under distribution shift (a workload mixing uniform and clustered instances), a pre-registered confirmatory experiment finds that allocation guided by held-out sample statistics improves best-of-k by 11.5% (AM, primary endpoint; 95% CI [7.4, 19.7]) and 12.0% (SymNCO, replication) at equal evaluation budget, with the signal-acquisition cost not charged; a pre-registered negative control (POMO, an order of magnitude more robust to shift) shows -0.3% [-0.7, 0.24]. The gain exceeds a frozen distribution-label baseline by 4.2 points [1.9, 7.7]. An exploratory policy charging a 20-sample probe against the same budget retains 3.4% (AM) and 4.6% (SymNCO). We give a correction procedure and a reporting checklist, and release all data, code, and the pre-registration record.

#8703. Tech Report: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (231 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (231 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

It has been revealed that arXiv:2608.12253v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) for human-AI interaction usually trains the agent against a single large language model (LLM) that simulates the user. We show that agents trained this way can systematically fail to generalize, and we trace the failure to simulator collapse: the simulator LLM is mode-collapsed, and a policy trained against it learns narrow strategies that exploit the simulator's mode behavior; these strategies transfer poorly to unseen simulators and to real users. We formalize the collapse and propose two solutions. Verbalized Sampling, applied at inference time, samples each simulator reply from a verbalized response distribution. Co-Training, applied during training similar to self-play, co-evolves the simulator as the policy, so the policy cannot exploit the mode behavior. A population variant samples the simulator for each rollout from a pool of recent checkpoints. We validate both solutions on three benchmarks: Persuasion for Good, tau^2-bench, and CooperBench. Verbalized Sampling improves held-out success by up to 9% over single-simulator RL, and Co-Training pushes gains further to 14%; the human study shows similar gain on real users. Both solutions also preserve the policy diversity that collapses under single-simulator RL. Overall, our findings on simulator collapse point to diverse simulators as a requirement for RL agents that serve real users. We release SCOPE, an open-source framework for Population Co-Training in multi-agent RL.

#8700. Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (261 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Semantic Prism: Generative Segmentation with an Explicit Semantic-Image Interface

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (261 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2608.11537v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Conditional image generators can render segmentation maps as semantic RGB images, but color drift and boundary mixing can undermine direct decoding. We present Semantic Prism, a framework that combines an explicit semantic-image interface with hierarchical refinement for road-scene segmentation. A generator adapted from a diffusion-distilled backbone produces a semantic RGB image with a single denoising upgrade per crop. Distances to a fixed class-color codebook define interface logits and pixelwise class probabilities. Hierarchical Generator Evidence Alignment (HGEA) combines spatially aligned multilevel features from the VAE encoder of the generator with the input image, generated semantic image, and interface probabilities to predict additive corrections to these logits. Contextual Interface Hierarchy Disagreement (C-IHD) combines pointwise uncertainty, local context, and interface-refinement disagreement in a fixed score for ranking pixel errors, without an auxiliary predictor or an additional network pass. On the 500-image Cityscapes validation set, Semantic Prism achieves 72.07% mean mIoU, improving on direct-interface decoding by 11.39 percentage points. Extensive capacity-matched ablations show higher mean mIoU for multilevel refinement than for flat and single-level alternatives. The Cityscapes-trained model transfers to ACDC Dataset, achieving 46.89% mIoU without target-domain adaptation. Beyond Cityscapes, on BDD100K dataset, a separately trained model achieves 62.22% mIoU on its full 1,000-image validation set. Across the 3 evaluated datasets, C-IHD improves pixel-error area under the AUPR over uncertainty derived from maximum softmax probability, with segmentation predictions held fixed for each comparison. In particular, on ACDC, AUPR increases from 0.6580 to 0.7557, demonstrating that Semantic Prism presents more effective error ranking under adverse-condition domain shift.

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (266 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (266 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2608.10450v4 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Software systems accumulate dependencies and design commitments over time, while the agents that modify them operate within bounded sessions. How, then, can development remain cumulative across generations of transient agents? We introduce EvoX Genesis, which organizes development as a persistent recursive software world. Agents enter an accepted repository version, delegate work within local scopes, and submit changes for verification and parent review. Once accepted, those changes pass to later episodes together with the contracts and tests used to assess them. The project thus preserves both earlier work and a basis for evaluating what comes next. We examine this continuity through four studies of formation, continuation and redevelopment. Starting without compiler code, Genesis built a C compiler with 219,676 lines of Rust source through 1,019 agent episodes over 123.4 hours. Within this growing implementation, repairs increased passes on a fixed set of 100 Csmith programs from 61 to 93; a subsequent revision retained all 93 passes. Development also continued in a separate compiler lineage when DeepSeek V4 Flash inherited a GLM 5.2 snapshot. To examine continuity when the implementation itself changes, Genesis redeveloped selected MESA functionality in Rust, with numerical agreement assessed against the Fortran reference across six workloads. The WebGL trajectory, meanwhile, exposed both repairs and regressions as repeated checks recorded progress towards 2,017/2,019 conformance pages passed. A complementary EvoX Compiler case connects program-merging performance to executable graph and backend contracts. Together, these records trace how accepted work becomes a foundation for further development: later agents inherit both usable implementations and concrete ways to assess further revisions.

Role Steering of Language Models for Social Simulations

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (185 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2608.00023v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Social simulations built from language-model agents need role-conditioned behavior that can be checked before agents are placed into a simulated population. We introduce an activation-steering screening workflow for role-conditioned agents: define a role profile, extract a role-specific direction, sweep four steering coefficients, evaluate role-profile alignment, and pass or flag each candidate configuration. On OLMo-3-7B-Instruct, we apply the workflow to a mixed 275-role inventory with 228 role-agnostic questions, GPT-4.1-mini prompted role references, and GPT-4.1-mini judges. We also introduce CastVectors, which receive higher judged role-profile alignment than an assistant-axis directional control from prior persona-vector work, with mean overall scores of 63.2 versus 41.1 across the tested grid. They also preserve high lexical diversity, while the control drops sharply at larger coefficients. The role-level screen is the main contribution: most roles improve as steering increases, but 38 roles decline across all six measured dimensions, showing why simulation builders should choose coefficients per role rather than deploy a uniform high-strength setting. Our code is available at https://github.com/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors, and the role vectors and evaluation data at https://huggingface.co/datasets/HCAI-Lab-GT/casting-call-vectors.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, digital sovereignty is evolving from a standard compliance requirement into a powerful strategic advantage for regulated industries worldwide.
  • Historically, achieving that level of control meant accepting an impossible tradeoff: rely on rigid legacy architectures that lacked access to frontier AI innovation, or stitch together brittle, manual guardrails that slowed developer velocity.
  • It has been revealed that google Cloud Data Boundary helps remove that compromise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Engineering Director, Regulated Cloud.

Group Product Manager, Regulated Cloud.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, digital sovereignty is evolving from a standard compliance requirement into a powerful strategic advantage for regulated industries worldwide. From European frameworks designed to meet sovereign standards (DORA, EHDS, GDPR) to FedRAMP/ILs/ITARs in the U.S., or expanding mandates across Asia-Pacific and the Middle East, organizations can build deeper global trust through clear governance over data locality, encryption keys and system access.

Historically, achieving that level of control meant accepting an impossible tradeoff: rely on rigid legacy architectures that lacked access to frontier AI innovation, or stitch together brittle, manual guardrails that slowed developer velocity.

It has been revealed that google Cloud Data Boundary helps remove that compromise. Built directly onto Google Cloud’s global commercial infrastructure, Data Boundary delivers software-defined, AI-assisted governance. This allows organizations to move at commercial speed with verifiable sovereign controls built in from day one. Today, we’re announcing a new and updated experience in Data Boundary.

Google Cloud Data Boundary combines technical controls across residency, access, and encryption with ongoing monitoring and operational assurance.

Sources indicate that data Boundary streamlines how security, data and AI teams configure, test and scale governance across their cloud footprint. Below are the key highlights for the latest experience:.

End-to-end visibility into sovereign controls: Browse and deploy pre-configured regional and industry frameworks with clear visibility into mapped technical controls, severities and remediation steps.

Flexible hierarchy-wide enforcement: Apply preventative guardrails across organizations, complex nested folders and projects — on both net-upcoming and existing workloads — to block out-of-policy API calls and configuration drift.

Dry run posture validation: Dry run any framework in monitor mode across live existing workloads to identify drift and violations before enabling active enforcement.

Compliance customization: Frameworks and controls customization according to your organization's needs. Use Gemini in Google Cloud to customize controls and generate remediation logic to help reduce manual compliance toil.

Accelerated compliance with machine-readable evidence: Continuously monitor posture, record immutable exception justifications, run scheduled audits and export machine-readable audit evidence to help fast-track certification workflows.

Turn compliance and digital sovereignty into a business accelerator.

Industry observers note that in an era of evolving global regulations and rapid AI transformation, compliance and sovereignty should accelerate your innovation, not hold you back. Google Cloud Data Boundary helps you  deploy frontier AI, scale globally across commercial regions, and meet stringent regulatory requirements — with greater control and visibility over your data, your keys and your operations.

Here are six steps to get started with Data Boundary today:.

You can access the Data Boundary directly from your Google Cloud console. Navigate to the Compliance tab in your Google Cloud console, and select Frameworks to begin with.

Select existing or configure your own compliance: Browse 40+ public sector, industry and sovereign AI control packages, or customize guardrails to match your specific organizational policies.

Select your regions: Designate precise geographic boundaries and data residency restrictions across 29 global commercial regions.

Evaluate workloads in dry-run mode: Enforce controls at either the folder or the project level. If you already have an active BigQuery or Gemini project running, you can turn on dry run mode to evaluate how controls behave across existing resources without disrupting live workloads.

Monitor against drifts and violations: Continuously track posture in real time to automatically detect non-compliant API calls and configuration drift without disrupting engineering velocity.

On-demand audits, scanning and compliance evidence generation: Export machine-readable evidence packages and audit-ready reports directly into your compliance workflow to accelerate Authorities to Operate (ATOs).

For a comprehensive guide on using Data Boundary, please refer to our detailed product documentation.

RecHarness: A Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for Self-Evolving Recommender Systems

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (184 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2607.29241v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Optimizing recommender models remains heavily reliant on manual iteration over architectures, objectives, and training strategies. While LLM-based agents can automate this trial-and-error process, relying on LLMs to both select modification directions and formulate concrete hypotheses can lead to unstable search under limited trial budgets. Inspired by the above challenge, we propose RecHarness, a Bandit-Routed Agentic Harness for automated recommender model optimization. RecHarness decouples the optimization process into two steps: a bandit router selects the next modification direction according to historical validation feedback, while the LLM generates a concrete optimization hypothesis and executable code edit within the selected direction. To sustain long-horizon exploration, RecHarness uses a jump-basin mechanism to activate a structural-jump arm when local edits stagnate. Across multiple recommendation tasks, datasets, and model backbones, RecHarness achieves more consistent performance improvements and uses limited trial budgets more effectively than LLM-directed search. During a 7-day online A/B test on a large-scale short-video advertising platform, the selected candidate improves ADVV by 2.084%, Revenue by 0.534%, and Exposure by 0.559%. Code is available at: https://github.com/6lyc/RecHarness.
